headline: High: shared filesystem/MCP and overlapping writes make prompt injection, leakage, and state corruption plausible by default.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Claude Code reads/writes repo files and uses MCP; TREK also uses MCP and exposes collaborative, real-time inputs. A can ingest file content as trusted instructions, and B can surface attacker-controlled content through shared files or MCP. The pair lacks provenance controls in the profiles, so injection is plausible even without a documented direct bridge.
conditions: IF either agent consumes shared file or MCP content as instructions without provenance checks, injection is possible.
IF TREK forwards user-authored travel content into Claude Code prompts, the attack path opens.
mitigations: Disable MCP on one side for the shared workflow.
Separate the agents into distinct workspaces.
Add a provenance tag to all cross-agent content.
Require manual review before any file-derived instruction is executed.

B_data_leakage.rationale: A handles git credentials and broad filesystem contents; B handles API keys, MFA secrets, reservations, and documents. Both can access files and networked services, so sensitive data can flow from shared workspace into either agent’s outputs or remote calls. The profiles do not show isolation or DLP, making leakage a default-risk concern.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same directory or synced files, sensitive material can be exposed to both.
IF either agent uploads file contents or context to external services, secrets may leave the local boundary.
mitigations: Use separate directories and separate credentials.
Redact secrets before either agent reads shared files.
Block network egress for files containing secrets.
Move sensitive artifacts to a non-shared vault.
Review logs for accidental secret inclusion.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A can write the filesystem, modify git state, and spawn subprocesses; B is collaborative and also uses files and MCP. If they touch the same repo or workspace, concurrent writes and git mutations can overwrite each other or corrupt state. No locking or coordination primitive is documented, so the conflict risk is high.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same repository or shared directory, state conflicts can occur.
IF either agent commits or rewrites git state while the other is active, history corruption or lost work is possible.
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate checkout.
Serialize git writes with a lock file.
Disable auto-commit or auto-merge paths.
Use branch-per-agent workflows.
Snapshot the workspace before concurrent runs.

D_cascading_error.rationale: A can generate code or file edits that B may consume in a collaborative workflow, while B can act on travel plans, reservations, and documents. The profiles do not prove B blindly trusts A, but the real-time collaborative setup makes unverified handoff plausible. This is a default-pathway concern rather than a guaranteed failure.
conditions: IF B treats A-produced files or notes as authoritative, downstream actions can be wrong.
IF A writes structured outputs that B renders or executes without verification, errors cascade.
mitigations: Insert a human verification step between agents.
Require B to cite source data before acting.
Mark A outputs as untrusted drafts.
Add schema validation for exchanged artifacts.
Limit A to suggestions, not final actions.

E_compliance.rationale: A is a closed-source Anthropic terminal agent handling git credentials and local files; B is a self-hosted travel planner handling reservations, email addresses, country visit history, and MFA secrets. The pair can mix sensitive travel data with code/workspace data, creating retention and residency ambiguity. The profiles do not document a direct residency mismatch, so medium is the cautious choice.
conditions: IF regulated travel data is copied into the shared workspace, retention and access controls may diverge.
IF either agent logs secrets or documents outside the intended jurisdiction, compliance obligations may be breached.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared folders.
Disable verbose logging for sensitive sessions.
Document retention rules for both systems.
Use separate storage for travel records and code.
Review jurisdiction and DPA requirements before syncing data.
